## False Negatives and False Positives (Type I and Type II Errors)


::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="60%"}

- Most diagnostic statistics seek to identify two types of errors:

  - *False Positive* ($\alpha$, Type I) refer to the probability that you will claim an effect is *present* when the **null hypothesis is true**.
  - *False Negatives* ($\beta$, Type II) refer to the probability that you will claim an effect is *absent* when the **null hypothesis is false**.

- Power is what is left over from a false negative error: $\text{power} = 1 - \beta$.

:::

::: {.column width="40%"}

![Dr. Jacob Cohen (1923-1998)](./images/cohen.png){#fig-cohen fig-alt="alt" height=50%}


:::

:::

\begin{center}
Power is \textbf{the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is in fact false and should be rejected.}
\end{center}


## Type S and Type M Errors

- Underpowered studies do more than miss real effects: when they *do* find a significant effect, that estimate is likely to be wrong.
- A significant estimate can be wrong in two ways:
  - *Type S (sign)*: the estimate has the opposite sign of the true effect. At $6\%$ power, $24\%$ of significant estimates do.
  - *Type M (magnitude)*: the estimate overstates the true effect. At $6\%$ power, significant estimates are $9.5$ times too large on average.

\vspace{0.4em}

\scriptsize Source: Gelman and Carlin (2014), \textit{Beyond Power Calculations: Assessing Type S (Sign) and Type M (Magnitude) Errors}.

## What Power Looks Like

```{r power-picture, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=7.6, fig.height=2.75, dev="png", dpi=300, fig.align="center"}
library(ggplot2)
cv <- qnorm(0.975)
zz <- seq(-3.6, 6.2, length.out = 700)
dd <- rbind(
  data.frame(z = zz, y = dnorm(zz, 0), curve = "If the null is true"),
  data.frame(
    z = zz,
    y = dnorm(zz, 2.24),
    curve = "If the 7-point effect is real"
  )
)

ggplot(dd, aes(z, y)) +
  geom_area(
    data = subset(dd, curve != "If the null is true" & z >= cv),
    fill = "#4A90C2",
    alpha = 0.55
  ) +
  geom_area(
    data = subset(dd, curve == "If the null is true" & z >= cv),
    fill = "#B41E1E",
    alpha = 0.70
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = curve), linewidth = 0.75) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = cv,
    colour = "grey20",
    linewidth = 0.4,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 3.6,
    y = 0.20,
    label = "power = 0.61",
    colour = "#0B2E52",
    size = 3.1,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 2.45,
    y = 0.045,
    label = "alpha/2 == 0.025",
    parse = TRUE,
    colour = "#B41E1E",
    size = 2.7,
    hjust = 0
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = cv,
    y = 0.43,
    label = "reject to the right of 1.96",
    colour = "grey20",
    size = 2.7,
    hjust = -0.04
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "If the null is true" = "#B41E1E",
      "If the 7-point effect is real" = "#0B2E52"
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  # 1.96 and 2.24 nearly collide on the axis; drop the second label a row
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(0, cv, 2.24),
    labels = c("0", "1.96", "\n2.24")
  ) +
  labs(x = "Effect, measured in standard errors", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(linewidth = 0.25, colour = "grey88"),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "grey30"),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.margin = margin(t = -6)
  )
```

\vspace{-0.2em}

\begin{center}
\footnotesize \textcolor{errorred}{\textbf{Red}} is the study you would run if there were no effect; the shaded sliver past 1.96 is $\alpha$ --- the false positives you agreed to tolerate. \textcolor{statsecondary}{\textbf{Blue}} is the study you expect if the effect is real; \textbf{the shaded area past the same line is power}.
\end{center}


## Traditional Statistical Power & Its Ingredients
\vskip0pt plus 1filll


So what do we need to actually calculate this? Well, the constituent components to calculate $1 - \beta$ are: 

* \textbf{$\alpha$, the significance criterion}
* \textbf{$N$, the sample size} 
* \textbf{$\delta$, the population effect size}
\vskip0pt plus 1filll

\begin{center}
\textit{So,} you must be thinking, \textit{what's the formula?!}

\end{center}

## Traditional Statistical Power & Its Ingredients 

\begin{center}
\Large
There isn't a formula for the calculation of power. There are many!
\end{center}

## Core Notation

In order to estimate statistical power, we need four properties:

\vspace{0.5em}

\begin{center}
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{7pt}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}
\begin{tabular}{c>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.1cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{7.9cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Symbol} & \textbf{Quality} & \textbf{What it is} \\
\midrule
$N$              & Sample size        & How many subjects you collect in total. \\
$\mu_t - \mu_c$  & Effect size        & The true difference between the treatment and control means: the \textit{signal}. \\
$\sigma$         & Standard deviation & How much outcomes vary from one another: the \textit{noise}. \\
$\alpha$         & Significance level & The Type I error rate you are willing to tolerate; it sets the evidence threshold. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\vspace{0.4em}

\begin{center}
\small Note we will use $\mu_t - \mu_c$ throughout to denote effect size. Where space is tight --- in code, and in the appendix --- we abbreviate it $\delta$. 
\end{center}


## The Three Ingredients of Statistical Power

\vspace{0.5em}

\begin{center}
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{7pt}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}
\begin{tabular}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.3cm}cc>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{6.2cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Ingredient} & \textbf{Symbol} & \textbf{Control?} & \textbf{What it does} \\
\midrule
Strength of the treatment & $\mu_t - \mu_c$ & Partly & Dose, framing, and duration are yours to set; a stronger treatment is easier to detect. \\
Background noise & $\sigma$ & Partly & Noisier outcomes bury the signal, but better measurement and covariates quiet it. \\
Experimental design & $N$, $\alpha$ & \textbf{Yes} & Sample size, randomization scheme, and covariate adjustment. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

## Let's look at a case where we can find a closed form

The formula depends entirely on what *specific* test you want to run. Here's an example. Let's make the following assumptions: 

1. We have a completely randomized experiment, with two groups are selected to form a binary treatment, each group containing $N \ 2$ 
2. Assume the outcome variable is normally distributed, and the control group has mean $\mu_c$ and the treatment group has $\mu_t$
3. The two groups have a shared standard deviation, $\sigma$

We now say we want to perform a difference of means test, in the two-tailed sense

## Let's look at a case where we can find a closed form

Say we have the following hypothetical situation where we want to compute power:

- A school is piloting a new **tutoring program**, and wants to know if it improves end-of-term test scores (out of 100)
- Students are randomized into two groups, with one half getting tutoring
- Untutored students average $\mu_c = 72$
- The school will consider the program "worth it", if tutoring gets average scores to $\mu_t = 75$
- Scores vary with $\sigma = 10$

## Let's look at a case where we can find a closed form

Say we have the following hypothetical situation where we want to compute power:

- A school is piloting a new **tutoring program**, and wants to know if it improves end-of-term test scores (out of 100)
- Students are randomized into two groups, with one half getting tutoring
- Untutored students average $\mu_c = 72$
- The school will consider the program "worth it", if tutoring gets average scores to $\mu_t = 75$
- Scores vary with $\sigma = 10$

\begin{center}
Luckily, in such a simple form, there's a nice asymptotic approximation for the power of the experiment
\end{center}

## Step 1: Do the Arithmetic

\vspace{0.2em}

\begin{align*}
\text{power} &= \Phi\!\left( \frac{|\mu_t - \mu_c|\sqrt{N}}{2\sigma} \;-\; \Phi^{-1}\!\left(1-\frac{\alpha}{2}\right) \right)
   && \text{\small the formula} \\[0.25em]
&= \Phi\!\left( \frac{7\,\sqrt{164}}{2(20)} \;-\; \textcolor{statsecondary}{1.96} \right)
   && \text{\small plug in; \;\; $\Phi^{-1}(0.975) = 1.96$} \\[0.25em]
&= \Phi\!\left( \textcolor{statsecondary}{\mathbf{2.24}} \;-\; 1.96 \right) \;=\; \textcolor{statsecondary}{\Phi(\mathbf{0.28})}
   && \text{\small $7 \times 12.81 / 40 = 2.24$}
\end{align*}

\vspace{0.5em}

\begin{center}
\small
$\underbrace{\mathbf{2.24}}_{\text{what you expect}}$ \qquad
$\underbrace{\mathbf{1.96}}_{\text{what you need}}$ \qquad
$\underbrace{\mathbf{0.28}}_{\text{all the room you have}}$
\end{center}

\vspace{0.5em}

\begin{center}
\scriptsize A thin margin means an unreliable study. One lookup turns $\Phi(0.28)$ into a number. \\
(Where does $1.96$ come from? Running the $z$-table \textit{backwards} --- see the appendix.)
\end{center}


## Step 2: Read the Answer Off the Table

\begin{columns}[T]

\begin{column}{0.30\textwidth}
\vspace{0.6em}

\begin{center}
$\text{power} = \Phi(\mathbf{0.28})$
\end{center}

\vspace{0.5em}

\footnotesize
Split the $z$-score across the two margins of the table:

\vspace{0.4em}

\hspace{0.5em}$\mathbf{0.2}\;$ selects the \textbf{row}

\vspace{0.2em}

\hspace{0.5em}$\mathbf{0.08}$ selects the \textbf{column}

\vspace{0.5em}

The cell where they meet is the area to the \textit{left} of $z$, which is exactly the power.
\end{column}

\midrule

\cellcolor{stataccbg}\textbf{0.2} & \cellcolor{stataccbg}.5793 & \cellcolor{stataccbg}.5832 & \cellcolor{stataccbg}.5871 & \cellcolor{stataccbg}.5910 & \cellcolor{stataccbg}.5948 & \cellcolor{stataccbg}.5987 & \cellcolor{stataccbg}.6026 & \cellcolor{stataccbg}.6064 & \cellcolor{statorange}\textbf{\color{white}.6103} & \cellcolor{stataccbg}.6141 \\
0.3 & .6179 & .6217 & .6255 & .6293 & .6331 & .6368 & .6406 & .6443 & \cellcolor{stataccbg}.6480 & .6517 \\

\vspace{0.5em}

\begin{center}
\large $\text{power} \;=\; \Phi(0.28) \;=\; \textcolor{statorange}{\mathbf{0.61}}$
\end{center}


## The Smallest Effect This Study Can See

\small We now know what this design does with a 7-point effect. The next question is what it \textit{can} do: fix power at 80\% and solve the same formula for the effect instead of for power.

\vspace{0.3em}

\begin{center}
$\displaystyle \text{MDE} \;=\; \underbrace{\left(\Phi^{-1}\!\left(1-\tfrac{\alpha}{2}\right) + \Phi^{-1}(0.80)\right)}_{1.96 \;+\; 0.84 \;=\; 2.80} \;\times\; \underbrace{\frac{2\sigma}{\sqrt{N}}}_{\text{standard error}}$
\end{center}

\vspace{0.3em}

\begin{center}
\scriptsize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{9pt}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.08}
\begin{tabular}{ccc}
\toprule
$N$ & \textbf{Smallest detectable effect} & \textbf{In standard deviations} \\
\midrule
\textcolor{statorange}{\textbf{164}} & \textcolor{statorange}{\textbf{8.75 points}} & \textcolor{statorange}{\textbf{0.44$\sigma$}} \\
257  & 6.99 & 0.35$\sigma$ \\
400  & 5.60 & 0.28$\sigma$ \\
800  & 3.96 & 0.20$\sigma$ \\
1396 & 3.00 & 0.15$\sigma$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\vspace{0.3em}

\begin{center}
\small Pilot assumes $\mu_t - \mu_c = \mathbf{7}$. \qquad This design detects $\textcolor{statorange}{\mathbf{8.75}}$ and up.
\end{center}


## Check: Put 8.75 Back Through the Formula

\vspace{0.2em}

\begin{align*}
\text{power} &= \Phi\!\left( \frac{8.75\,\sqrt{164}}{2(20)} \;-\; 1.96 \right)
   && \text{\small the MDE in place of the pilot's effect} \\[0.25em]
&= \Phi\!\left( \textcolor{statsecondary}{\mathbf{2.80}} \;-\; 1.96 \right) \;=\; \Phi(\textcolor{statsecondary}{\mathbf{0.84}})
   && \text{\small $8.75 \times 12.81 / 40 = 2.80$} \\[0.25em]
&= \mathbf{0.80}
   && \text{\small row $0.8$, column $.04 \to .7995$}
\end{align*}

\vspace{0.4em}

\begin{center}
\footnotesize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{9pt}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.15}
\begin{tabular}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{6.6cm}c}
\toprule
\textbf{Pin these three} & \textbf{Get} \\
\midrule
$N = 164$, \; $\sigma = 20$, \; effect $= 7$      & power $= 0.61$ \\
$N = 164$, \; $\sigma = 20$, \; power $= 0.80$    & effect $= 8.75$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}



## Your Turn: Is the Tutoring Program Worth Studying?

\vspace{0.5em}

\begin{notebox}
\small A colleague is evaluating a new tutoring program. \textbf{400 students} will be randomly assigned, 200 to tutoring and 200 to business as usual, with final exam score as the outcome. Past cohorts averaged \textbf{72} points with a standard deviation of \textbf{10}, and the program is expected to add \textbf{3} points.
\end{notebox}

\vspace{0.7em}

\begin{center}
\large \textbf{What is the power of this design?}
\end{center}

\vspace{0.7em}

\begin{columns}[c]

\begin{column}{0.46\textwidth}
\begin{center}
\footnotesize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{10pt}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.2}
\begin{tabular}{cc}
\toprule
\textbf{Symbol} & \textbf{Value} \\
\midrule
$N$      & 400  \\
$\mu_t$  & 75   \\
$\mu_c$  & 72   \\
$\sigma$ & 10   \\
$\alpha$ & 0.05, two-sided \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{column}

\begin{column}{0.50\textwidth}
\footnotesize
The formula and the $z$-table are on your \textbf{handout}.

\vspace{0.6em}

Work it in three moves:

\vspace{0.3em}

\hspace{0.4em}1. Compute what you \textbf{expect}

\vspace{0.2em}

\hspace{0.4em}2. Subtract what you \textbf{need}

\vspace{0.2em}

\hspace{0.4em}3. Look the difference up
\end{column}

\end{columns}



## Your Turn: The Solution

\vspace{0.2em}

\begin{align*}
\text{power} &= \Phi\!\left( \frac{|75 - 72|\,\sqrt{400}}{2(10)} \;-\; \Phi^{-1}\!\left(1-\tfrac{0.05}{2}\right) \right)
   && \text{\small \textbf{Step 1:} plug in} \\[0.25em]
&= \Phi\!\left( \frac{3 \times 20}{20} \;-\; 1.96 \right)
   && \text{\small \textbf{Step 2:} $\sqrt{400} = 20$; $\Phi^{-1}(0.975) = 1.96$} \\[0.25em]
&= \Phi(3.00 - 1.96) \;=\; \textcolor{statsecondary}{\Phi(\mathbf{1.04})}
   && \text{\small \textbf{Step 3:} simplify} \\[0.25em]
&= \mathbf{0.85}
   && \text{\small \textbf{Step 4:} row $1.0$, column $.04 \to .8508$}
\end{align*}

\vspace{0.2em}

## Reading the Power Curve

\begin{columns}[c]

\begin{column}{0.53\textwidth}

\begin{itemize}
\item The $x$-axis is \textbf{total sample size}; the $y$-axis is \textbf{power}.
\item The blue curve traces power as $N$ grows, holding the effect at 3 and $\sigma$ at 10.
\item The red dashed line marks the \textbf{80\% target}. Where the curve crosses it is the $N$ you need (here \textbf{349}).
\item Our $N = 400$ sits to the \textit{right} of that crossing. Reading up from 400 gives $\approx \mathbf{0.85}$.
\item The curve \textbf{flattens}: past $\sim$600 suggests diminishing returns at larger N.
\end{itemize}
\end{column}

\end{columns}

## Where to Situate Power Analysis in Your Research

- Power analysis is tricky because we need information about our data to derive power (e.g., $\sigma$, $\mu_t - \mu_c$).
- The problem is power calculations are most useful *before* we've collected our data!
- In order to do power analysis we need to do some educated guessing: 
  - How big an effect should I anticipate? 
  - How many people can I realistically afford to treat?
  - How many subjects will answer my survey?

## What If We Don't Know the Effect?

\vspace{0.2em}

\small Back to the survey experiment. The pilot fixed everything \textit{except} for the anticipated effect size.

## The Formula, in Code

```{=latex}
\vspace{0.6em}

\begin{center}
$\displaystyle \text{power} \;=\; \Phi\!\left( \frac{|\mu_t - \mu_c|\sqrt{N}}{2\sigma} \;-\; \Phi^{-1}\!\left(1-\frac{\alpha}{2}\right) \right)$
\end{center}

\vspace{0.9em}
```

```{r power-fn, echo=TRUE}
power_calc <- function(mu_t, mu_c, sigma, N, alpha = 0.05) {
    z <- abs(mu_t - mu_c) * sqrt(N) / (2 * sigma)
    cv <- qnorm(1 - alpha / 2)
    pnorm(z - cv) + pnorm(-z - cv) # both rejection tails
}
```

```{=latex}
\vspace{0.9em}

\begin{center}
\large $\Phi \;=\;$ \texttt{pnorm} \qquad\qquad $\Phi^{-1} \;=\;$ \texttt{qnorm}
\end{center}
```


## Power Across a Range of $N$

```{r sweep, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
grid <- expand.grid(N = seq(60, 1600, by = 10), delta = c(3, 5, 7))

grid$power <- power_calc(
    mu_t = 50 + grid$delta,
    mu_c = 50,
    sigma = 20,
    N = grid$N
)

head(grid, 3)
```

```{=latex}
\vspace{0.4em}

\begin{center}
\small One formula, three assumptions, `r nrow(grid)` rows. Now plot \texttt{power} against \texttt{N}.
\end{center}
```


## How Many Respondents Do We Need?

```{r sweep-plot-setup, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
grid$delta <- factor(grid$delta, levels = c(3, 5, 7))
nstar <- data.frame(delta = factor(c(3, 5, 7), levels = c(3, 5, 7)))
nstar$N <- ceiling((2 * 20 * (qnorm(0.975) + qnorm(0.80)) / c(3, 5, 7))^2)
nstar$power <- 0.80
ramp <- c("3" = "#4A90C2", "5" = "#1F5F8B", "7" = "#0B2E52")
```

```{r sweep-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7.4, fig.height=3.3, dev="png", dpi=300, fig.align="center"}
ggplot(grid, aes(N, power, colour = delta)) +
    geom_hline(
        yintercept = 0.80,
        linetype = "dashed",
        colour = "#B41E1E",
        linewidth = 0.4
    ) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.85) +
    geom_point(data = nstar, size = 1.9, colour = "#B41E1E") +
    geom_text(
        data = nstar,
        aes(label = N),
        vjust = 1.9,
        hjust = -0.15,
        size = 3,
        colour = "#B41E1E",
        show.legend = FALSE
    ) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = ramp, name = "Assumed effect (points):") +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.05), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.2)) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1600, 200)) +
    labs(x = "Total respondents (N)", y = "Power") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major = element_line(linewidth = 0.25, colour = "grey88"),
        axis.title = element_text(colour = "grey30"),
        legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.margin = margin(t = -4),
        legend.key.width = unit(16, "pt"),
        legend.title = element_text(colour = "grey30")
    )
```

## Your Turn: One Solution

```{r exercise-solution, echo=TRUE}
grid <- expand.grid(N = seq(50, 1000, by = 10), delta = c(0.10, 0.15, 0.20))
grid$power <- power_calc(
    mu_t = 3.05 + grid$delta,
    mu_c = 3.05,
    sigma = 0.45,
    N = grid$N
)

for (d in unique(grid$delta)) {
    ok <- grid$N[grid$delta == d & grid$power >= 0.80]
    cat("effect", d, "GPA points -> N =", min(ok), "\n")
}
```

\footnotesize Your effects and $N$ range will differ. The *structure* is the answer: one grid, one call, one threshold.

## But what about literally any other case? 

There are lots of reasons why, even for simple problems, we don't want to rely on such an approximation. For instance, what if you

1. don't assume a two-tailed test? 
2. have clustering and want some sort of random effect? 
3. are taking a Bayesian approach? 
4. are using nonparametric statistics?

## What should we do in those other cases?

* Even when power is not as clearly defined, there are still a whole range of things we still want to know about "power"
* Let's start relaxing our definition of power. We can, for now, consider it as: 

\vskip50pt 


\begin{center}
\textbf{The probability that we we \textcolor{red}{recover} a real effect, should one \textcolor{red}{exist}}
\end{center}

## What should we do in those other cases?

What would it mean then, to approach asking questions about power or sample size in a more general sense where we may want to consider:

\vskip20pt 
::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="60%"}

* Non-parametric approaches
* Bayesian approaches
* Or even just moderately more complicated study designs? 

\vskip20pt 

\begin{center}
\textbf{Well, we go gambling}
\end{center}

:::

::: {.column width="40%"}

![Oxford Casino Hotel](./images/casino.png){#fig-casino fig-alt="alt" height=50%}


:::

:::

## An aside into the casinos at Monaco

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="60%"}

* Monte Carlo refers to a broad class of methods wherein you use repeated random sampling to obtain some form of numerical result 
* It will be very useful for us when we cannot rely on a closed form solution (which, as a reminder, is in most cases!)
* Essentially, we can use \textcolor{red}{randomness} to solve \textcolor{red}{deterministic} problems

\vskip20pt 

\textit{For any problem with probabilistic interpretation, it can be solved with Monte Carlo}

:::

::: {.column width="40%"}

![Primary developer of the MC method, Stanisław Ulam, who was inspired by his uncle's gambling](./images/ulam.png){#fig-casino fig-alt="alt" height=50%}

:::

:::


## An aside into the casinos at Monaco

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="60%"}

Let's imagine we want to know the answer to a gambling-related problem with a closed-form answer:

\begin{center}
What's the probability you win on red at the roulette table three spins in a row?
\end{center}
- There are 18 \textcolor{red}{red} pockets out of 38, so the exact answer is 

$$
P(\text{3 reds in a row}) = (18/38)^3 \approx 0.106
$$
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}

![A reasonably standard roulette table](./images/roulette.png){#fig-casino fig-alt="alt" height=50%}

:::

:::

## An aside to the casinos at Monaco

But we could also just... go to the casino 100,000 times:

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
set.seed(2026)
spins <- matrix(runif(3 * 100000) < 18 / 38, ncol = 3) # each row is 3 spins
mean(rowSums(spins) == 3) # proportion of rows where all three won
```

\begin{center}
If we can describe \textcolor{red}{how the data are generated}, we can estimate \textit{any} probability by running the process many times!
\end{center}

## An aside into the casinos at Monaco

\vskip0pt plus 1filll

\begin{center}
\Large
And whether its the more traditional, rigid form, or our more flexible modern form, power is \textit{just a probability.}
\end{center}

\vskip0pt plus 1filll

## So, how do we do a Monte Carlo simulation, anyways?

In the parametric context, a Monte Carlo power analysis looks like this:

1. **Generate** random data from some distribution with the properties that you expect your real data to have
2. **Analyze** this randomly generated data set with your statistical analysis, whatever that is
3. **Store** the value(s) of the analysis that you're interested in
4. **Repeat** the above steps many times
5. **Compute** power by looking at the proportion of times the statistic or value you're interested in was "correct"

\vskip20pt

\begin{center}
This can be arbitrarily complex or simple!
\end{center}

## So, how do we do a Monte Carlo simulation, anyways?

We can consider all of this to be done, for the sake of simplicity, by three piecemeal functions that we will want to write

- `generate()`: make a fake data set that looks like your study
- `analyze()`: run the analysis you'd *actually* run
- `success()`: decide whether this run "recovered" the effect

and one function that necessarily performs the actual simulation

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
simulate_power <- function(n_sims, generate, analyze, success) {
    hits <- replicate(n_sims, success(analyze(generate())))
    mean(hits) # proportion of successful runs = power
}
```

## So, how do we do a Monte Carlo simulation, anyways?

We need to make a statement on how we think the data are being generated. For student $i$:

$$
\text{post}_i = \underbrace{\mu_c}_{\text{baseline}} + \underbrace{\delta \, T_i}_{\text{tutoring effect}} + \underbrace{\varepsilon_i}_{\text{noise}}, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)
$$

\vskip10pt

- $\mu_c = 72$: the average score *without* tutoring
- $T_i$: 1 if student $i$ was tutored, 0 if not, so tutored students get an "effect" of $\delta = 3$
- $\varepsilon_i$: our random noise with $\sigma = 10$

\vskip10pt

## So, how do we do a Monte Carlo simulation, anyways?

Let's start with our function that generates data based on our student tutoring example from before.

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
gen_basic <- function(n = 350, effect = 3, sd = 10) {
    treat <- rep(0:1, each = n / 2) # half control, half tutored
    post <- 72 + effect * treat + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = sd)
    data.frame(treat, post)
}

head(gen_basic())
```


## So, how do we do a Monte Carlo simulation, anyways?

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(2026)
dat <- gen_basic()

ggplot(
  dat,
  aes(x = post, fill = factor(treat, labels = c("Control", "Tutored")))
) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(72, 75), linetype = "dashed") + # true means
  labs(x = "End-of-term score", y = "Density", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## So, how do we do a Monte Carlo simulation, anyways?

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
analyze_lm <- function(dat) {
  fit <- lm(post ~ treat, data = dat) # same as an equal-variance t-test
  summary(fit)$coefficients["treat", ] # estimate, SE, t, p for treat
}

success_sig <- function(est) {
  est[["Pr(>|t|)"]] < 0.05 # did we reject the null?
}

analyze_lm(gen_basic())
```

## Does the casino agree with our nice equation??

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
set.seed(2026)
simulate_power(
    n_sims = 2000,
    generate = gen_basic,
    analyze = analyze_lm,
    success = success_sig
)
```

\vskip10pt

- Pretty close for only 2000 simulations! 


## Does the casino agree with our nice equation??

- It's worth noting that the simulation has its own error! With $S$ simulations, the Monte Carlo standard error is

$$
\text{SE} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{S}}
$$

\begin{center}
Want a more precise answer? \textbf{Go to the casino more times.}
\end{center}

## What if we make this more complicated, arbitrarily so?

I suspect that schools know a lot about their students *before* the program starts. Say we also have each student's **pre-test score**. Our model for student $i$ becomes:

$$
\text{pre}_i \sim N(70, \sigma^2)
$$

$$
\text{post}_i = \underbrace{\mu_c}_{\text{baseline}} + 
\underbrace{\rho\,(\text{pre}_i - 70)}_{\text{what we knew already}} + 
\underbrace{\delta \, T_i}_{\text{tutoring effect}} + 
\underbrace{\varepsilon_i}_{\text{noise}}, 
\qquad \varepsilon_i \sim N\big(0,\ \sigma^2(1-\rho^2)\big)
$$

\vskip05pt

- $\rho = 0.6$ is the correlation between pre-test and end-of-term scores
- Students who were above average before tend to stay above average
- The total spread of scores is still $\sigma = 10$

## What if we make this more complicated, arbitrarily so?

* We only need to change **two** of our three pieces:

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
gen_pretest <- function(n = 350, effect = 3, sd = 10, rho = 0.6) {
  treat <- rep(0:1, each = n / 2)
  pre <- rnorm(n, mean = 70, sd = sd)
  post <- 72 +
    rho * (pre - 70) +
    effect * treat +
    rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = sd * sqrt(1 - rho^2))
  data.frame(treat, pre, post)
}

analyze_ancova <- function(dat) {
  summary(lm(post ~ treat + pre, data = dat))$coefficients["treat", ]
}
```

## What if we make this more complicated, arbitrarily so?

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
set.seed(2026)
simulate_power(2000, gen_pretest, analyze_lm, success_sig)
simulate_power(2000, gen_pretest, analyze_ancova, success_sig)
```

\vskip10pt

- We can see that our power jumps from about 80\% to about **94\%**
- Power is a property of the \textcolor{red}{design \textit{and} the analysis}, not just of $N$
- If we were really strapped for students to enroll, this could be really helpful to know!

\small
(To be fair: this case still has a closed form ($\sigma$ just becomes $\sigma\sqrt{1-\rho^2}$) but we didn't need to know that!)

## Let's make it even **more** complicated! 

Consider the classic problem of dropout. Let's make the following assumptions about our study (maybe we base this on some sort of past experience running such a study):

- Students who are doing *badly* are more likely to stop showing up
- The **control group loses more students** (here, about 23\% vs. 11\%)

\vskip20pt

\begin{center}
You may ask: \textit{Is there a formula for the power of this study?} \\
\vskip5pt
\textbf{Not really.} Dropout depends on an \textit{unrealized outcome}, so the \textcolor{red}{sample size}, the \textcolor{red}{effect we estimate}, \textit{and} the \textcolor{red}{noise} all change at once!! What a pain!!
\end{center}

## Let's make it even **more** complicated! 

But we don't need a formula! We can use our computers!! We just need to describe how the data are generated:

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
gen_dropout <- function(n = 350, effect = 3, sd = 10, rho = 0.6) {
    dat <- gen_pretest(n, effect, sd, rho)
    p_drop <- plogis(-2.2 + 0.7 * (dat$treat == 0) - 0.12 * (dat$post - 72))
    dat[runif(n) > p_drop, ] # we only observe the students who stayed
}

nrow(gen_dropout()) # out of the 350 we enrolled
```

## Let's make it even **more** complicated! 

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
set.seed(2026)
simulate_power(2000, gen_pretest, analyze_ancova, success_sig)
simulate_power(2000, gen_dropout, analyze_ancova, success_sig)
```

\vskip10pt

- Remember, dropout doesn't just shrink our sample!

## Let's make it even **more** complicated! 

Because we simulated the data, we *know* the true effect is 3. So we can check:

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
set.seed(2026)
estimates <- replicate(2000, analyze_ancova(gen_dropout())[["Estimate"]])
mean(estimates)
```

\vskip10pt

- Since students doing poorly *leave*, this biases our results for the control group up
- We appear to **underestimate** the effect

\begin{center}
Unfortuantely, there's no formula for this!!
\end{center}

## Let's make it even **more** complicated! 

Remember our relaxed definition: \textbf{the probability that we \textcolor{red}{recover} a real effect, should one \textcolor{red}{exist}}.

* "Recover" doesn't have to mean a p-value. 

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
success_close <- function(est) abs(est[["Estimate"]] - 3) < 1.5

set.seed(2026)
simulate_power(2000, gen_pretest, analyze_ancova, success_close) # no dropout
simulate_power(2000, gen_dropout, analyze_ancova, success_close) # dropout
```

## Let's make it even **more** complicated! 

\large
There are other options for recovery! You could ask when: 

* the CI excludes zero
* the CI is narrower than some width
* the sign is right
* a posterior probability exceeds 0.9 or 0.95
* and much more!

## So, how many students do we need?!

Just like before, we want to find the $N$ that gets us to 80\%. Now, instead of inverting a formula, we try a grid of sample sizes:

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
set.seed(2026)
ns <- seq(150, 500, by = 50)
powers <- sapply(ns, \(n) {
  simulate_power(
    1000,
    generate = \() gen_dropout(n = n),
    analyze = analyze_ancova,
    success = success_sig
  )
})
```

## So, how many students do we need?

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.5
plot(
  ns,
  powers,
  type = "b",
  pch = 19,
  ylim = c(0, 1),
  xlab = "Students enrolled (N)",
  ylab = "Simulated power"
)
abline(h = 0.8, lty = 2, col = "red")
```

\begin{center}
\small With dropout, we need to enrol \textbf{around 450 students}. Alas, more students only buys \textit{power} because the estimate is \textcolor{red}{still biased}.
\end{center}

## Your turn!

We provided you with a template file to use for htis part, \texttt{power-sim-template.R}. Use this and fill in every \texttt{\_\_\_}. Use your own study, or, if nothing comes to mind, the tutoring study from earlier is good practice too!

Ask yourself:

1. What are my baseline, effect, and noise values, and where did I get those numbers?
2. \texttt{generate()} -- Does this dataset look like something my study could produce?
3. \texttt{analyze()} -- What would I \textit{actually} run on the real data? 
4. \texttt{success()} --  What counts as "recovering" the effect? 
5. Estimate power -- With \textit{no} effect, do I get about 5\%? A significance-based \texttt{success()} should succeed about 5% of the time
6. Perform a sweep over $N$ -- Where does my curve cross 80\%? 
7. Now, \textcolor{statsecondary}{\textbf{add a complication}} -- Maybe unequal groups, a covariate, a skewed outcome, with these how much power do I lose?
